lead: A shaft that has run for years can break at a stress well below yield. The load repeats, so a tiny crack starts at a notch, grows a little each cycle, and finally snaps the remaining metal. Fatigue design asks one question: for a given stress amplitude, how many cycles will the part survive? The S–N curve answers it. The endurance limit gives the amplitude below which steel seems to last indefinitely. You meet this in shafts, springs, bolts, axles and any part under rotation or vibration.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.2 for Kf and notch sensitivity, and Unit 1 for fully reversed bending stress and stress amplitude.

blocks.text: Fatigue is failure under a stress that repeats. The stress amplitude is Sa = (σmax − σmin)/2. The mean stress is σm = (σmax + σmin)/2. Fully reversed loading has σm = 0, so Sa = σmax. A part can carry a static stress below yield and still fail after many cycles. Fatigue happens in three stages.

Stage 1, crack initiation. Cyclic slip inside grains forms persistent slip bands. The surface develops intrusions and extrusions. A notch, keyway, thread root or corrosion pit raises the local elastic stress by the theoretical stress concentration factor Kt times the nominal stress. The fatigue notch factor Kf = 1 + q(Kt − 1), where q is the notch sensitivity, is the smaller factor by which the fatigue strength or endurance limit is reduced, so the crack starts earlier at the notch. Chapter 2.2 explains Kt, Kf and notch sensitivity.

Stage 2, stable crack growth. The crack moves across the section a little on every cycle. In some metals the fracture face shows striations, one stripe per cycle. Beach marks are larger lines where the load changed or the crack paused; they are not cycle-by-cycle stripes.

Stage 3, final fracture. The remaining section is too small, so one overload breaks it. The fracture face then has a rough fast-fracture zone. Fatigue design tries to keep the part in stage 1 or to count cycles before stage 2 becomes unsafe.

The R. R. Moore rotating bending test measures fatigue. A polished specimen of circular section is rotated under a constant bending moment. Every surface point sees a fully reversed sinusoidal bending stress. The tester counts cycles N until the specimen breaks. The test repeats at several stress amplitudes S.

Plot S against N on log–log axes. For steel the points lie near a straight line from about (10³, 0.9Sut) to (10⁶, Se). Here Sut is the ultimate tensile strength in MPa and Se is the endurance limit in MPa. The line is S = A N^b. S is the stress amplitude in MPa, N is cycles, A is a constant in MPa, and b is the slope per decade, a negative number. From the two points, b = [log₁₀(Se) − log₁₀(0.9Sut)] / (6 − 3) = (1/3) log₁₀(Se/(0.9Sut)). Finite life follows from the same line: N = (S/A)^(1/b), or log₁₀ N = log₁₀(S/A)/b.

Ferrous metals show a knee at about 10⁶ cycles. Below Se they survive many more cycles, so Se is a true endurance limit. Aluminium, copper and most non-ferrous metals have no knee. Their S–N line keeps falling, so a fatigue strength at a stated life is used instead of an endurance limit. Some syllabi place the steel knee at 10⁷ cycles; use the value your data gives.

Se' is the endurance limit of a polished, small, bending specimen. For steels up to about Sut = 1400 MPa, Se' = 0.5Sut. Above that, use about 700 MPa. The real part is not the test specimen, so apply Marin factors: Se = ka kb kc kd ke Se'.

ka is the surface finish factor. A machined surface is lower than a polished one; a forged or corroded surface is lower still. kb is the size factor. In a larger section the stress gradient is flatter and a bigger volume of material is highly stressed, so a weak spot is more likely; kb therefore falls as the diameter rises. kc is the load factor. Bending is the reference, kc = 1.0. Axial loading and torsion give lower values. kd is the temperature factor. It is 1.0 at and below room temperature; the endurance limit falls as temperature rises well above room temperature (roughly above 200–250 °C for steel). ke is the reliability factor; a 90% reliability gives ke below 1.0, and higher reliability gives a smaller ke. Use the charts or tables in your data book.

Surface treatment changes fatigue strength more than bulk strength. Polishing removes scratches. Shot peening puts the surface in compression, so a crack must first overcome that compression; it raises fatigue strength. Corrosion pits and sharp notches act as small cracks and lower it. The S–N curve here is for fully reversed constant amplitude stress. Mean stress needs the Goodman, Soderberg or Gerber line in Chapter 2.4.

figure.caption: The S–N line falls from 540 MPa at 10³ cycles to 230 MPa at 10⁶ cycles and then stays flat at the endurance limit. The short level line marks Se = 230 MPa from 10⁶ to 10⁷ cycles.

spec.aria: An S–N line falling from 540 MPa at a thousand cycles to 230 MPa at a million cycles and then staying flat as the endurance limit; a short level line marks the endurance limit from a million to ten million cycles.

examples.question: A machined steel shaft has Sut = 600 MPa. The surface factor is ka = 0.85, the size factor is kb = 0.90, and the load, temperature and reliability factors are all 1.00. The shaft carries a fully reversed bending stress amplitude of 300 MPa. (a) Find Se'. (b) Find Se. (c) Find the fatigue life N in cycles.
steps: Check the steel range: Sut = 600 MPa is below about 1400 MPa, so Se' = 0.5Sut = 0.5 × 600 = 300 MPa.
Apply Marin factors: Se = ka kb kc kd ke Se' = 0.85 × 0.90 × 1.00 × 1.00 × 1.00 × 300 = 229.5 MPa. Take Se = 230 MPa for the S–N line.
The line passes through (10³, 0.9Sut) = (10³, 540 MPa) and (10⁶, 230 MPa). Slope b = [log₁₀(230) − log₁₀(540)] / (6 − 3) = −0.1236 per decade.
examples.answer: Se' = 300 MPa, Se = 229.5 MPa (taken as 230 MPa), and the life at 300 MPa is about 1.16 × 10⁵ cycles.
examples.check:
import math
Sut = 600.0
Se_prime = 0.5 * Sut
Se_raw = 0.85 * 0.90 * 1.0 * 1.0 * 1.0 * Se_prime
Se = round(Se_raw)
b = math.log10(Se / (0.9 * Sut)) / 3.0
logN = 3.0 + math.log10(300.0 / (0.9 * Sut)) / b
N = 10 ** logN
print(f'{Se_prime:.1f}')
print(f'{Se_raw:.1f}')
print(f'{Se:.1f}')
print(f'{b:.4f}')
print(f'{logN:.2f}')
print(f'{round(N, -3):.1f}')

traps: Se' = 0.5Sut is not the design endurance limit. It is the polished specimen value; multiply by all five Marin factors for the actual part.
Do not use an endurance limit for aluminium or most non-ferrous metals. They have no knee; use fatigue strength at the required life.
The S–N line from a rotating bending test is fully reversed bending. A mean stress moves the failure point; use Chapter 2.4.
Beach marks are not striations. Beach marks are macroscopic arrest lines; striations are one per cycle under a microscope.
Use log₁₀ consistently: b = Δlog₁₀S / Δlog₁₀N, so over 3 decades log₁₀S changes by 3b. Do not mix log₁₀ with ln, and do not read b as a change in S per cycle.

quiz.q: In the R. R. Moore rotating bending test, what is the mean stress and what is the stress amplitude?
quiz.a: The mean stress is zero. The stress amplitude equals the bending stress at the specimen surface; the loading is fully reversed.

quiz.q: Define endurance limit Se for steel.
quiz.a: Se is the stress amplitude below which a steel specimen survives the stated number of cycles, usually 10⁶ for the knee, without fatigue failure.

quiz.q: Why does a sharp notch reduce fatigue life more than it reduces static strength?
quiz.a: The notch raises the local elastic stress by Kt. The fatigue notch factor Kf is the smaller factor by which the endurance limit is reduced, so a crack starts earlier at the notch.

quiz.q: Why is there no true endurance limit for aluminium?
quiz.a: The S–N curve for aluminium has no knee. It keeps falling as cycles increase, so a fatigue strength at a stated life is used instead of a stress below which failure never occurs.

quiz.q: A steel has Sut = 700 MPa, ka = 0.80, kb = 0.90, and kc = kd = ke = 1.00. Find Se' and Se.
Shot peening raises fatigue strength but barely changes tensile strength. Explain.
quiz.a: Shot peening puts the surface in compressive residual stress. A fatigue crack must overcome this compression before it can open and grow, so crack initiation is delayed. The bulk tensile strength is unchanged.

quiz.q: A fracture face shows beach marks but no visible striations. What can you say about the failure?
quiz.a: Beach marks show crack growth under changing load or crack arrest. Striations may be absent in some alloys or too fine to see. The part still failed by fatigue; beach marks alone do not give a cycle count.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, fatigue life is estimated with rainflow counting of real load histories, then Miner's rule for cumulative damage; that is the next step after constant amplitude S–N. Fracture mechanics uses the Paris law, da/dN = C(ΔK)^m, to track crack growth. Automotive axles, wind turbine shafts and railway wheels are tested on servo-hydraulic rigs. Search for fatigue crack growth, rainflow counting and fatigue notch factor to go further.
